content: When magnesium sulfate is administered at higher doses in combination with central nervous system (CNS) depressants, there is an increased risk of enhanced CNS depression. This necessitates close monitoring for signs of excessive sedation or respiratory depression. Magnesium sulfate and potassium chloride, when co-administered with medications such as quinapril, quinidine, quinine, ramipril, ribociclib, rifampin, risedronate, risperidone, rocuronium, sacubitril/valsartan, salsalate, samidorphan, sertraline, sevelamer, sodium polystyrene sulfonate, sotalol, streptomycin, succinylcholine, sucralfate, sucroferric oxyhydroxide, sulindac, telmisartan, tetrabenazine, thioridazine, thiothixene, tiludronate, tobramycin, tobramycin inhaled, tolmetin, torsemide, trandolapril, triamcinolone acetonide (both extended-release and injectable forms), trientine, trifluoperazine, trimipramine, valsartan, vandetanib, vardenafil, vecuronium, ziprasidone, zoledronic acid, alendronate, aluminum hydroxide, amikacin, amikacin liposome inhalation, amiodarone, amitriptyline, amoxapine, amphotericin B (cholesteryl sulfate, deoxycholate, and liposomal forms), and other agents, may lead to increased toxicity or potentiation of effects. The mechanisms of these interactions vary, including QTc interval prolongation, potentiation of neuromuscular blockade, or other undefined pathways. For medications that prolong the QTc interval (e.g., quinidine, ribociclib, sotalol, vandetanib, vardenafil, tetrabenazine, thioridazine, ziprasidone), there is a heightened risk of serious cardiac arrhythmias. It is recommended to consider pre-dose and post-colonoscopy electrocardiograms (ECGs) in patients at increased risk of arrhythmias. For medications that cause fluid and electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., sacubitril/valsartan, rifampin, risedronate, sevelamer, sodium polystyrene sulfonate, sulindac, telmisartan, torsemide, trandolapril, valsartan, alendronate, aluminum hydroxide, amphotericin B formulations), co-administration with magnesium sulfate/potassium chloride may increase the risk of adverse events such as seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Close monitoring of fluid and electrolyte balance is advised. Magnesium sulfate may potentiate the effects of neuromuscular blocking agents (e.g., rocuronium, succinylcholine, vecuronium), leading to prolonged muscle relaxation or weakness. Monitoring for signs of excessive neuromuscular blockade is essential. For trientine, magnesium sulfate/potassium chloride can decrease its absorption in the gastrointestinal tract due to chelation. To mitigate this interaction, trientine should be administered at least one hour before or after magnesium sulfate/potassium chloride. For CNS depressants (e.g., risperidone, samidorphan, sertraline, thiothixene, trimipramine, amitriptyline, amoxapine, trifluoperazine), magnesium sulfate may enhance CNS depression. Patients should be closely monitored for signs of excessive sedation or respiratory depression. In summary, the co-administration of magnesium sulfate/potassium chloride with various medications requires careful consideration of potential interactions, close monitoring for adverse effects, and, in some cases, modification of therapy or dosing schedules.
